summary: This informational document clarifies terminology for Software-Defined Networking (SDN), an approach to running networks dynamically through open interfaces and software. It describes the layers and architecture commonly used to discuss SDN, so people use the same words for the same parts.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7426 provides terms for describing the parts of a Software-Defined Network and how they interact. It is a reference model for discussion, not a design that every network must implement.

subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the planes and abstraction layers used to describe SDN.

tldr.problem: People used Software-Defined Networking to describe different ideas and interfaces. The RFC organizes common terms for the layers, planes, and interfaces found in SDN architectures.
tldr.mechanism: It defines forwarding, operational, control, management, and application planes, along with four abstraction layers and the interfaces between them. It also classifies examples of SDN-enabling technologies using this model.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7426 is an IRTF taxonomy, not a standard or a specification of a particular architecture. It provides reference definitions without recommending one technology.

today: RFC 7426 is an Informational document from the IRTF, published in January 2015. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the document is a taxonomy rather than a standard.

sections.title: Software-Defined Networking
sections.content:
Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is a programmable-network approach in which software can control individual network devices and shape network behavior. A central idea is to abstract the forwarding plane so that the control plane can be separated from it.

The RFC notes that SDN definitions did not consistently describe layers and interfaces. OpenFlow and NETCONF, for example, had both been called SDN interfaces even though the RFC places them in different roles. Its purpose is to consolidate terminology, not to standardize a particular layer or interface.
sections.plainLanguage: SDN describes ways for software to program network devices through defined interfaces. This RFC provides shared names for the parts involved.

sections.title: The Planes in an SDN Model
sections.content:
The forwarding plane handles packets. The operational plane manages the working state of an individual device, such as its port and interface status. The control plane decides how one or more devices should forward packets, while the management plane monitors, configures, and maintains devices.

The application plane contains applications and services that program network behavior. The RFC uses resources to mean physical or virtual components, such as a port, queue, or complete network device. Applications use services; services expose APIs to applications or other services.
sections.plainLanguage: The forwarding plane moves packets, while the control plane decides how they should move. The management plane looks after devices, and the application plane contains software that uses network services.

sections.title: Abstraction Layers and Interfaces
sections.content:
The Device and resource Abstraction Layer (DAL) presents device resources to control and management functions. The Control Abstraction Layer (CAL) gives control applications access to the Control-Plane Southbound Interface. The Management Abstraction Layer (MAL) gives management applications access to the Management-Plane Southbound Interface.

The Network Services Abstraction Layer (NSAL) exposes services to applications and other services. Interfaces can be APIs or inter-process communication when entities share a device, or protocols when they are separate. Layers can be stacked recursively, and planes may be together or physically separated.
sections.plainLanguage: Abstraction layers give each plane a consistent way to reach device resources or services. The interfaces can be software calls inside one device or protocols between separate devices.

sections.title: Control Plane and Management Plane
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes control from management by what each does, how quickly it acts, and how long its state lasts. Control-plane updates may be needed roughly every few milliseconds and often concern temporary state such as routing. Management-plane work may take minutes, hours, or days and often changes persistent configuration.

Traditionally, control was distributed and local to devices, while management was centralized and remote. SDN controllers can blur that distinction by making control logically centralized. The RFC also discusses the CAP theorem: a centralized controller can provide a consistent view, but losing connectivity to it can make a flow unavailable until the connection returns.
sections.plainLanguage: The control plane handles frequent forwarding decisions, while management usually changes settings less often. Centralizing control can make it harder for devices to keep working when they lose contact with the controller.

sections.title: Using the Model to Classify Technologies
sections.content:
The RFC uses its terminology to describe technologies that expose or model network functions. ForCES and OpenFlow are examples associated with the control-plane southbound interface; YANG can model device resources, while NETCONF is a management protocol. The RFC describes OpenFlow version 1.4.

Other examples include SNMP, which uses management information bases to describe managed data, and PCEP, which supports communication between path computation elements. The RFC's aim is to place technologies in a common taxonomy, not to compare their quality or recommend when to deploy them.
sections.plainLanguage: The model helps readers describe what role a technology plays, such as controlling forwarding or configuring a device. The RFC does not choose a preferred technology.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 7426 proposes no new network architecture or protocol, so it says the taxonomy has no impact on Internet security. It emphasizes that security still matters when someone designs or operates a network using SDN, and points to the documents for specific interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC names and organizes SDN concepts but does not define a new protocol. Security requirements belong to the architectures and interfaces built using those concepts.
